NY-2025-A10052.s: The law extends the town of Red Hook’s power to charge a tax on real estate sales and put that money into a community preservation fund. It was signed into law on October 23, 2026. The extension runs through December 31, 2051.

NY-2025-A10162.s: This law extends a limit on how much the share of taxable property can shift between classes in the town of Orangetown in Rockland County. For certain assessment rolls, the current base proportion of any class cannot be more than 1% higher than the previous year’s amount, if the town has passed a local law, ordinance, or resolution allowing it. If needed, the town’s legislative body must adjust the class proportions so their total equals one.

NY-2025-A10201.s: This law exempts the village of Williamsville fire department in Erie County from the rule that non-resident members cannot be more than forty-five percent of the department. It affects the membership rules for that fire department.

NY-2025-A10376.s: Utility companies would have to tell customers about planned rate increases at least 30 days before the new price takes effect. They would also have to give contact information and a way to cancel service completely. The bill would affect utility service providers and their customers in New York.

NY-2025-A10568.s: This bill would create a program to give financial assistance to covered water systems for the abatement, removal, and replacement of lead-contaminated water lines. To get money, a system would have to show proof that the work was completed and show the direct costs. The maximum reimbursement would be twelve thousand dollars per water line replaced, plus interest on certain loans, and some costs like attorney or administrator fees would not be reimbursed.

NY-2025-A10744.s: The bill makes the residential parking permit system in Buffalo permanent. It affects the city of Buffalo and the people who live and park there.

NY-2025-A10750.s: This bill would prohibit selling, offering for sale, distributing, or using pesticides with first-generation or second-generation anticoagulant rodenticides in New York, with some listed exceptions. It would also bar use of these pesticides within five hundred feet of a designated wildlife habitat area. The bill makes exceptions for certain certified pesticide applicators in specific agricultural settings and requires rules for the exceptions.

NY-2025-A10808.s: The bill would limit how government agencies use automatic license plate reader systems and the plate data they collect. It would block that use except for certain allowed purposes. It affects government entities that use these systems.

NY-2025-A10960.s: The bill would require election officials to tell domestic violence victims when the confidentiality on their voter registration records is about to end. The notice would also include information on how to apply again for confidential records. It was signed into law.

NY-2025-A10998.s: The bill makes technical fixes to a 1981 law about the Sag Harbor Volunteer Exempt Firemen's Benevolent Association, including changing the word “fireman” to “firefighter” and correcting some references. It affects that local firemen's benevolent association and its powers and duties, and it was signed into law.

NY-2025-A11321.s: This law changes where Washington County deputy county attorneys can live. It allows them to live in Washington County or in a nearby county in New York. It was signed into law on October 23, 2026.

NY-2025-A11373.s: This law extends the state rules on taking sharks. It changes the expiration date of those rules from December 31, 2026 to December 31, 2028. It affects people who fish for or catch sharks in New York.

NY-2025-A11377.s: The bill would extend rules on how many Jonah crabs can be taken for two more years. It affects people who harvest Jonah crabs in New York. It was signed into law as Chapter 330.

NY-2025-A11443.s: This law changes how commercial food fish licenses are issued in New York. It affects people and businesses that need those licenses to catch and sell food fish.

NY-2025-A11454.s: The law extends through December 31, 2027, a set of rules for Lower Manhattan construction work that cover joint bidding on public work contracts. It affects public work projects in that area and the contractors who bid on them.

NY-2025-A11455.s: This law extends the end date for rules on joint bidding for contracts on public work projects. It changes the current expiration date to December 31, 2027. It affects public work contracts in New York.

NY-2025-A11532.s: The bill extends certain rules for a Long Island deer management pilot program for 3 more years. It applies to that program and became law as Chapter 336.

NY-2025-A5175.s: The bill would require baby monitors that send audio or video over the internet to include certain security features to help block unauthorized access. It would also require a written warning label and set penalties for breaking the rule. It was signed into law.

NY-2025-A6338.s: The bill would expand the definition of a victim of a sexual offense to include someone harmed by the unlawful sharing or posting of an intimate image. It passed the Senate and was later signed into law as Chapter 364.

NY-2025-A6495.s: The bill would require school boards to make rules and steps for children and young teens at risk, including those who have shown suicidal thoughts, been bullied, or left school grounds without permission. It would also create a group to review the safety and security of children in public and private schools in New York. The measure affects primary and secondary school students and school systems.

NY-2025-A6790.s: This bill would raise the state tax credit for active volunteer firefighters and volunteer ambulance workers from two hundred dollars to eight hundred dollars for taxable years beginning on and after January first, two thousand twenty-six. It would also let a taxpayer get this credit even if they receive a related real property tax exemption. For spouses filing a joint return, the credit would be sixteen hundred dollars when both qualify.

NY-2025-A6836.s: The bill would let a person on a shared contract leave that contract with no fee, penalty, or charge if they are a domestic violence victim. It would also stop the company from shifting the remaining bill or contract duty to the other people on that shared contract. It would bar the company from refusing to let that person start a new contract later.

NY-2025-A7033.s: This law lets the state arts council name Little Yemen in New York City as a cultural district. It adds the area’s borders in the Bronx and keeps the council’s power to name other cultural areas that are compact and have a shared cultural heritage. The law took effect right away.

NY-2025-A7285.s: The bill would create a peer support mental health program for first responders, using support from other peers. It would affect first responders in New York.

NY-2025-A7366.s: The bill would require the state public service commission to audit some private water companies. It would also require certain companies that are under investigation to give public updates on how they are following orders. The measure is aimed at water utilities and their customers.

NY-2025-A7839.s: This law relates to the Nesconset Volunteer Exempt Firefighter's Benevolent Association. It sets out the group's purpose and how it may use foreign fire insurance premium tax money. It was signed into law on October 23, 2026.

NY-2025-A8796.s: The bill would let certain land parcels get an exemption from rules that limit how alcohol makers, wholesalers, and retailers can share an interest in a licensed place or sell alcohol for drinking on site. It affects certain manufacturers and wholesalers of alcoholic beverages and would end some related rules after a set time.

NY-2025-A8939.s: This law makes a lodging facility liable for a civil penalty if it does not comply with requirements for providing information about services for human trafficking victims. The penalty is five hundred dollars for a first offense and one thousand dollars for each later offense. A local or state agency must give reasonable notice of noncompliance and allow thirty days to fix the violation before collecting the penalty. The law also lets certain municipal officials enforce these rules, and the money collected is kept by the municipality or local government.

NY-2025-A9042.s: Veterinary clinics would have to give notice and documents to the attorney general before certain sales or other deals are completed. The attorney general would review whether the deal could hurt public access to veterinary care. It would also block some private contract terms that place negative limits on how a veterinary clinic can use its property or business.

NY-2025-A9184.s: The bill would limit when insurance companies, pharmacy benefit managers, and pharmacies can control each other. It would require some owners to give up part of their interest in one or more insurance companies or pharmacy benefit managers. If they break these rules, they could be barred from getting payment from certain state programs.

NY-2025-A9225.s: The bill would make it unlawful for a person to own, run, or control both a health insurance company and a health care provider, even in part. It would require people in that position to sell off one side within three years. Health insurance companies and health care providers that break these rules could lose payment from certain state programs.

NY-2025-A9232.s: The bill would allow remote electronic witnessing to be done with an electronic notarization and would help record deeds and other property papers signed electronically. It would also make electronic signatures valid on powers of attorney. This would affect people using these documents in New York.

NY-2025-A9568.s: Requires electric scooter service platforms to keep liability insurance and show proof that they have it. It would affect companies that run electric scooter services.

NY-2025-A9693.s: The bill would extend a set of rules on how people operate personal watercraft and specialty prop-craft, which are small watercraft with propellers. It would keep one part of that law in place until January 1, 2029, affecting people who use these watercraft in New York.

NY-2025-J2379.s: This resolution would honor James R. Peluso after his death for receiving a Liberty Medal, which is the New York State Senate's highest honor for a person. It would also send a copy of the resolution to his family. The measure is about recognition, not a new law or program.

NY-2025-J2380.s: This resolution would mourn the death of Dolores Huerta, a labor leader and civil rights advocate, and honor her work for working families, women, children, and other communities. It would also send a copy of the resolution to her family.

NY-2025-J2381.s: This resolution commends Corporal William L. Rood for receiving the New York State Senate Liberty Medal. It says he served in the Korean War, later worked for the Village of Canton Police Department and the Lawrence Ambulance Company, and was active in his community.

NY-2025-J2382.s: This resolution commends Lt. Colonel Barbara Caldara for being named a recipient of a Liberty Medal from the New York State Senate. It says she served in the United States Army, worked as a nurse, and later worked for Greene County Public Health Family Planning for more than 20 years. It also notes her volunteer work and community activities, and that a copy of the resolution will be sent to her.

NY-2025-J2384.s: This resolution commends Brigadier General Barry Hartman for being named a recipient of a Liberty Medal from the New York State Senate. It also says he served in the U.S. Army and the New York Guard and lists his military service and awards.

NY-2025-J2385.s: This resolution commends Specialist Ruben Cespedes for receiving a Liberty Medal from the New York State Senate. It says he is a United States Army veteran from Freeport, New York, who was injured while serving in Afghanistan and later continued public service as a sergeant with the New York Police Department.

NY-2025-S10187.s: The bill would change the name used from "firemen" to "firefighters" in the rules for the Volunteer and Exempt Firefighter's Benevolent Association of Bethpage. It would also direct that certain taxes sent to the group be used to support its stated purposes. The bill was signed into law.

NY-2025-S10244.s: The bill would change how certain money received by the West Babylon Volunteer Firemen's Benevolent Association can be used. It would also update old gendered language to newer wording. The bill passed both houses and was signed into law.

NY-2025-S10526.s: The bill lets Yates County assistant district attorneys, except the first assistant district attorney, live in Monroe County instead of only in Yates or certain nearby counties. It also lets Yates County assistant public defenders live in Monroe County. The change takes effect immediately.

NY-2025-S10586.s: The bill became law and extends the rules on public hearings for proposed rules until January 1, 2028. It affects the state rulemaking process, which is how agencies make new rules.

NY-2025-S10643.s: The bill would change rules for labor peace agreements in the cannabis industry and the cannabis industry wage board. It affects cannabis businesses and workers in that industry. It was signed into law on 2026-10-28.

NY-2025-S10663.s: This bill would change New York rules for reporting independent expenditures. It expands what counts as an independent expenditure, adds definitions for “entity” and “true source,” and requires more disclosure about who gave money and where it came from. It also bars some funds from being used until required information is reported and raises civil penalties for failing to identify independent expenditures or political communications.

NY-2025-S10698.s: The bill would change how children qualify for health care by removing household income as a factor. It would affect rules for deciding who can get this coverage.

NY-2025-S10716.s: The bill would direct the state Department of State to set up free public courses to help people train for state certified real estate appraiser, state licensed real estate appraiser, and appraiser assistant licenses. It would affect people who want to enter those jobs in New York.

NY-2025-S10717.s: The bill would exempt 116th Street in Manhattan, between Riverside Drive and FDR Drive, from some camera-based enforcement rules tied to bus lanes and bus operations. It would affect drivers and bus traffic on that stretch of street.

NY-2025-S10718.s: The bill would create the "Prader-Willi syndrome residential stabilization and best-practice support act." It would provide services to people with Prader-Willi syndrome and help support their residential care.

NY-2025-S10719.s: The bill would create a temporary commission to study and make recommendations on Legionnaires' disease cases linked to cooling towers in New York City. The commission would end when its term expires, and the law would be repealed then.

NY-2025-S10720.s: Creates a learning module about tickborne illnesses in New York. It would be for state medical colleges and universities, county health departments, and the public.

NY-2025-S10721.s: The bill would let a person choose to self-exclude from online gambling platforms only, instead of from both online and in-person gaming sites. It would change New York rules for the state’s self-exclusion list and the steps for adding or removing someone from it. The change would take effect right away.

NY-2025-S10722.s: The bill would ban non-compete deals and some other work limits for healthcare workers. It would also let covered healthcare workers sue an employer or other person in court if they think the rule was broken.

NY-2025-S10723.s: The bill would let a person charged with a noncriminal traffic ticket from riding a bicycle or electric-assist bicycle choose to watch a safety video approved by the state commissioner instead of paying a fine. It would apply to people cited for these bicycle traffic violations.

NY-2025-S10725.s: The bill would require at least one automated external defibrillator to be available at electric utility worksites where two or more utility workers are doing work on high-voltage transmission or distribution lines. It would also require electric utilities to keep emergency response plans for using these devices.

NY-2025-S10726.s: The bill would let the village clerk of Alden live outside the village if they live in a nearby county next to Erie County. It affects the village clerk in Alden, New York.

NY-2025-S10727.s: The bill would stop cooperative housing programs from taking bad actions or retaliating against shareholders. It affects people who own shares in those housing programs.

NY-2025-S10728.s: The bill would require the state homeland security agency to run a statewide check of critical infrastructure, like important systems and facilities. It would look for weak spots, test how reliable and ready the systems are, and make recommendations to lower risks to public health, safety, security, and the economy. These assessments would have to happen at least once every three years.

NY-2025-S10729.s: The bill would make the state motor vehicle agency check that a penalty record really matches the driver before taking action. It would let drivers contest a suspension, revocation, or other penalty if they think it is a case of mistaken identity. Any penalty would be put on hold until a final decision is made.

NY-2025-S10730.s: The bill would require Medicaid to cover applied behavior analysis therapy given during school hours in certain schools. It would affect people on Medicaid who get this therapy at school.

NY-2025-S10731.s: The bill would change New York rules for training and using advanced artificial intelligence models under the RAISE Act. It affects people and companies that build or use these frontier AI models. The change is meant to update those AI safety and education rules.

NY-2025-S10732.s: The bill would create minority youth-owned business enterprises in New York state and New York City. It would also set up contracting chances for members of these businesses. In addition, it would create a program to carry out the plan and an oversight committee to watch it.

NY-2025-S10733.s: This bill would add a new law on artificial intelligence liability. It would make developers of certain covered models strictly liable for injuries to non-users in some cases, and it sets rules for when an artificial intelligence system is treated as having the mental state needed for a tort. It also provides affirmative defenses for developers if the model met the same standard of care as humans doing the same function, or if the injury came from a capabilities failure that would not be negligence or an intentional wrong if done by a person.

NY-2025-S10734.s: This bill would make the board of regents the only state entity that can choose whether New York takes part in the federal scholarship tax credit program. It would also let the board of regents provide the state's list of qualified scholarship granting organizations. The commissioner of taxation and finance could not act to join the program unless the board of regents first makes that election.

NY-2025-S10735.s: This bill would require the attorney general’s law enforcement misconduct investigation office to review complaints about certain officers or employees when there are at least five complaints from five or more people about at least five separate incidents within two years. If the office finds a pattern or practice of misconduct, excessive force, or dishonesty, it would send those findings to district attorneys for review of related misdemeanor cases. District attorneys would then review each identified case and decide whether dismissal, modification, consent to vacatur, further investigation, or no further action is warranted. The bill says it would not require automatic dismissal or vacatur of any charge or conviction.

NY-2025-S1443.s: This law lets the town justice in Rushford, Allegany County, live outside the town, as long as they live somewhere else in Allegany County. It changes the state rules on town justice residency for that town. It took effect right away.

NY-2025-S184.s: The bill would set up a one-year job training and work program for eligible young people ages 16 to 24. The state office in charge of temporary aid would run the pilot in 3 local social services districts, and one would be in New York City.

NY-2025-S1851.s: This bill would create a New York Main Street development center within the Empire State Development Corporation. The center would work with other state agencies to share information on existing state programs for redeveloping Main Street buildings. It would also provide technical and training help, create a web page with links to state, local, and federal programs, and keep a library of Main Street development publications.

NY-2025-S5057.s: This bill would increase the state subsidy for school lunch meals for school food authorities that bought at least thirty percent of their food products from New York state farmers, growers, producers, or processors in the previous school year. The subsidy would apply to school breakfast service, lunch service, and reimbursable snack program purchases, and schools would have to apply each year. The Department of Agriculture and Markets and the State Education Department would handle the application, review, certification, and payment process.

NY-2025-S5691.s: Allows the town justice in West Almond, in Allegany County, to live outside the town as long as they still live in Allegany County. The bill was signed into law.

NY-2025-S597.s: Would require New York’s public service commission to audit certain private water companies. It would also require some of those companies, when under certain investigations, to file public updates on how they are following orders. The measure targets certain private water companies.

NY-2025-S6396.s: This bill would let people ask for a nonapparent disability notation on non-driver ID cards, drivers’ licenses, and learners’ permits without having to provide proof. It would also let a person ask to remove that notation later, and the department would delete records tied to it. The department would not share this information with insurers or use it for medical review or fitness-to-drive referrals. The bill says a nonapparent disability includes all intellectual and developmental disabilities, and the card would show a discreet butterfly mark.

NY-2025-S7012.s: Health care providers would have to help arrange a screening for maternal depression before a mother leaves the birthing facility and at the first postnatal visit, unless the mother refuses. The screening would also have to be covered by insurance.

NY-2025-S7204.s: This law exempts the Caughdenoy Volunteer Fire Department, Inc. in the town of Central Square, Oswego County from the 45% limit on non-resident members. It changes the rules for who may be members of that fire department. The rest of the membership rules in the law still apply.

NY-2025-S7236.s: The bill would bar someone from buying ammunition if they failed a background check, are blocked by federal law, or are under a temporary or extreme risk protection order. It applies to ammo buyers in New York. The bill was signed into law as Chapter 316.

NY-2025-S7920.s: The bill would let a court make an order for a destitute minor that clears the way for adoption and gives guardianship and custody to the social services commissioner so they can consent to the adoption. It would also let certain social services agencies and public welfare officers give that consent. It affects children placed with local social services agencies as destitute minors.

NY-2025-S8102.s: This bill would require operating system providers for internet-enabled devices to conduct age assurance when a device is activated, and within one hundred eighty days for devices already activated. It would also require them to provide covered developers with a digital signal showing a user's age category, and covered developers would have to request that signal when a user downloads and launches an application. The bill includes rules on data deletion, encryption, family account applications, and enforcement by the attorney general.

NY-2025-S8276.s: The bill would let a person who does not live in Rockland County serve as an assistant county attorney there. It passed the Legislature and was signed into law as Chapter 340.

NY-2025-S8454.s: The bill became law and removes the local residency rule for the St. Lawrence County public health director and community services director. People in those jobs would not have to live in the county or other local area tied to the office.

NY-2025-S8666.s: This bill would set rules for youth sports organizations that organize, host, or oversee youth sports events. It would bar certain contract terms, including stay-to-play arrangements, exclusivity that blocks athletes from joining other youth sports organizations, and undisclosed penalties for leaving before a sports season ends. It would also require written cost disclosures, data privacy notices, and limits on restrictions about personal media at youth sports events. The bill would not apply to school-based sports programs and some Olympic-related athletic programs.

NY-2025-S8713.s: This bill would expand the definition of “reproductive health services” for the crime of criminal interference with health care services or religious worship in the second degree. It would also define “legally protected health activity” and keep the offense focused on force, threats, physical obstruction, or property damage tied to health care services or religious worship. The bill says a parent or legal guardian of a minor would not be prosecuted for conduct directed only at that minor.

NY-2025-S8719.s: This bill would create a tax credit for food service establishments that donate prepared meals to eligible community-based organizations, including food pantries. The credit would equal 50% of the fair market value of each qualified donation, up to $7 per donation, starting with the 2027 tax year. To claim it, the business would need to keep specific records about the donation. The bill also directs the agriculture and markets department to promote local ingredient procurement for these donated meals.

NY-2025-S8732.s: The bill would widen the area outside Montgomery County where a Montgomery County deputy sheriff may live. It passed the Assembly and was signed into law on October 23, 2026.

NY-2025-S8733.s: The bill would let people who serve as correction officers in Montgomery County live in certain other counties instead of only one place. It passed the Assembly, was sent to the governor, and was signed into law as chapter 344.

NY-2025-S9051.s: This law bars artificial intelligence companions from using features that are considered unsafe for minors. It also defines key terms and says which features count as unsafe. It applies to companies that make or run these AI companion tools in New York.

NY-2025-S9098.s: The bill would extend New York’s urban deer management pilot program for three more years. It affects the state program that helps manage deer in urban areas, and it was signed into law as Chapter 346.

NY-2025-S9153.s: The bill would add certain parcels of land to the list of places that are exempt from the usual rules that keep alcohol makers, wholesalers, and retailers from sharing part of the same liquor license. It affects manufacturers, wholesalers, and retailers at those specific locations. It was signed into law as Chapter 347.

NY-2025-S9197.s: Creates a not-for-profit group for eligible current and former volunteer members of the New Hartford Fire Department in Oneida County. The group may help injured, disabled, or needy members and their families, keep a meeting place, and run social and recreation activities. It also may receive certain fire insurance tax money for its work, and that part applies to premiums received on or after January 1, 2027.

NY-2025-S9205.s: This bill changes rules for appointing a guardian for personal needs or property management. It says a social services official or agency cannot be ordered to serve as guardian without written consent, and it gives that official or agency the right to take part in the proceeding if it is nominated or considered. It also requires certain banks and other financial institutions to provide bank statements and other records needed for a Medicaid or public assistance application within a reasonable time, and some must provide them within 30 days.

NY-2025-S9248.s: This law changes the residency rules for certain village officers in Washingtonville, Orange County. The village clerk, deputy village clerk, village treasurer, and deputy village treasurer may live in Orange County or an adjoining county in New York instead of having to live in the village. It also says these same offices in other villages still require village residency unless state law says otherwise.

NY-2025-S9866.s: Creates a public list of people who have broken certain illegal dumping laws, and keeps the list available for three years. The list would be public and would affect people found in violation of those dumping rules.

NY-2025-S9890.s: The bill would limit how government agencies can use automatic license plate readers and the plate data they collect. It would allow that use only for certain approved purposes. This would affect government entities that use these systems or handle the data.

NY-2025-S9947.s: This law updates how foreign fire insurance premium taxes are collected and used by the Centerport Volunteer Exempt Firefighter's Benevolent Association. Foreign fire insurance premium taxes are payments tied to some insurance policies sold by out-of-state insurers. It affects that local fire group in New York.

NY-2025-S9968.s: Creates the Harris Hill Volunteer Fire Company Benevolent Association. It sets rules for who can join, what the group can do, how it is set up, and how it handles money and property. It also covers payment of foreign fire insurance premium taxes, and it was signed into law as Chapter 354.

NY-2025-S9969.s: The bill would let the town justice in the town of Dix, in Schuyler County, live outside that town. It was signed into law as Chapter 355.

NY-2025-S9977.s: Makes technical changes to the law that created the Islip Terrace Volunteer Exempt Firefighter's Benevolent Association. The bill passed the Assembly, was sent to the Governor, and was signed into law as chapter 356.
